costGuide.title: BMW N62B40 Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting an N62B40 typically takes 12-14 hours at £65-£75/hr (independent BMW specialist) - main dealer rates are no longer applicable for this engine, as BMW no longer supports it through main dealer channels.
paragraphs: What genuinely moves the price for this engine is whether the valve stem seals have been addressed (a common failure leading to oil consumption), the condition of the alternator bracket gasket (a well‑known oil leak point), and the cooling system components (water pump, thermostat, coolant pipes). A reconditioned unit that includes these replacements will command a premium. See our full reconditioned engine cost guide for more detail.

failures.title: BMW N62B40 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Valve Stem Seal Wear - oil consumption and blue smoke on startup
items.whatHappens: The N62 engine family is notorious for valve stem seal wear, causing oil to seep past the seals into the combustion chamber. This results in blue smoke on cold starts, especially after the car has been sitting overnight. Over time, oil consumption increases, and carbon buildup on valves and catalytic converters can occur. The N62B40 is no exception to this well‑documented issue.
items.repairVsReplace: Valve stem seal replacement is a significant job (£1,500-£3,000) requiring cylinder head removal. If caught early, the repair is viable; if ignored, carbon buildup and catalytic converter damage can occur, potentially requiring a full engine replacement. Many owners opt for a reconditioned exchange unit that already has new seals fitted. Read our full valve stem seal guide

items.title: Alternator Bracket Gasket Oil Leak - common N62 oil leak
items.whatHappens: The N62's alternator bracket gasket is a known weak point, with oil leaking from the gasket and dripping onto the exhaust manifold, causing a burning oil smell. This is a very common failure across the N62 family, and the N62B40 is often affected. The gasket hardens and shrinks over time, leading to oil seepage.
items.repairVsReplace: Alternator bracket gasket replacement is a straightforward repair (£300-£600) if caught early. If left unaddressed, oil can accumulate and cause fires or damage to the alternator. It does not typically lead to engine failure, but it's a common annoyance. Read our full oil leak guide

items.title: Cooling System Leaks - water pump, thermostat, and coolant pipes
items.whatHappens: The N62's cooling system is under stress, with the water pump, thermostat, and various plastic coolant pipes prone to leaks and failure. The water pump impeller can fail, the plastic coolant pipes can crack, and the thermostat can stick, leading to overheating and potential head gasket failure.
items.repairVsReplace: Water pump and thermostat replacement typically resolves the issue (£500-£1,000 at an independent specialist). If overheating is ignored, head gasket failure can occur (£1,000-£2,500 to repair), or in severe cases, cylinder head damage requiring full engine replacement. Read our full cooling system failure guide

variants.title: N62B40 Sub‑Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: The N62B40 engine exists in multiple revisions across the production run. The two main sub‑codes are the early revision (N62B40A) and the later revision (N62B40B), which incorporated minor updates to gasket materials and engine management. - Fitted to: BMW E65/E66 740i (2002-2005), and early E60 540i (2005) - Key technical difference: Original gasket design; slightly different ECU calibration; early production N62 with known valve stem seal and gasket weaknesses - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares the family valve stem seal and oil leak issues; the early revision is more prone to gasket hardening and coolant pipe embrittlement due to age - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with N62B40B without ECU update; the later revision has revised gaskets and minor intake manifold differences - Fitted to: BMW E60 540i (2006-2007), E65/E66 740i (2005-2009) - Key technical difference: Revised alternator bracket gasket, updated water pump design, and improved valve stem seal material; still shares the same block and internals - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Valve stem seal wear is still present but typically less severe than the earlier revision; oil leaks from the alternator bracket gasket are less common - Interchange note: Can be swapped with N62B40A if the ECU is updated and the appropriate gaskets are used; but the later revision is generally preferred The engine code is stamped on a metal plate on the cylinder block, visible from the driver's side of the engine bay, and appears on the V5C registration document. The revision letter (A or B) is part of the full engine code. Alternatively, enter your registration above - we'll confirm your exact fitment.

relatives.description: - the older 4.0L V8 that preceded the N62 in the E39 540i and E38 740i; it features a different block design, conventional valvetrain (no Valvetronic), and Alusil cylinder linings. The M62 is generally considered more robust regarding valve stem seals, but it's heavier and less fuel-efficient.

- the 4.4L V8 that replaced the N62B40 in the E60 545i and E65 745i; it produces 333 hp and shares the same Valvetronic and VANOS architecture. It's a direct upgrade for N62B40 owners, though ECU and fuel system calibration differ.

- the 4.8L V8 sibling fitted to the E60 550i, E63 650i, and early E70 X5 4.8i; it produces 367 hp and is the most powerful naturally-aspirated N62 variant. If you're considering an upgrade, this offers the most power, but engine mounts, ECU, and cooling systems differ significantly.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement N62B40 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used N62B40 can make sense for owners of lower‑value E60 540i or E65 740i examples where a reconditioned unit would exceed the vehicle's value. However, used units carry significant risk: you don't know the valve stem seal condition, the alternator bracket gasket integrity, or the cooling system history. Only consider a used unit with documented service history and a compression test. Expect to pay £800-£1,800 for a used N62B40.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: For most N62B40 replacements, a professionally reconditioned unit is the right call. A proper recon addresses the engine's known weak points: the valve stem seals are replaced, the alternator bracket gasket is renewed, the cooling system (water pump, thermostat, coolant pipes) is overhauled, and all other gaskets and seals are replaced. With a 12‑24 month warranty, this is the lowest‑risk option for a £2,500-£4,000+ investment.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for this engine only when the original block is in good condition and the vehicle has significant sentimental or collector value - e.g. a low‑mileage E65 740i or a well‑specified E60 540i. A rebuild allows for upgraded internals and improved materials, but for most owners, a reconditioned exchange unit offers better value and less downtime. Expect £3,500-£5,500+ for a full rebuild.

items.question: What are the common problems with the N62B40?
items.answer: The most significant issues are valve stem seal wear (causing blue smoke on startup and oil consumption), alternator bracket gasket oil leaks, and cooling system failures (water pump, thermostat, coolant pipes). These are well-documented across the entire N62 family. A compression test and bore scope inspection are essential before buying any N62B40. Consider proactively replacing the cooling system if you're investing in a replacement engine.

items.question: How do I tell the N62B40 apart from the N62B44 and N62B48?
items.answer: The engine code is stamped on a metal plate on the driver's side of the cylinder block, and appears on the V5C and in the VIN (digits 4‑7). The N62B40 is a 4.0L V8 producing 306 hp; the N62B44 is a 4.4L V8 producing 333 hp; the N62B48 is a 4.8L V8 producing 367 hp. They share the same architecture but have different bore/stroke, ECU calibration, and fuel systems. The N62B40 and N62B44 have the same 89mm bore but different strokes. Fitting the wrong displacement variant requires a different ECU and engine loom.

items.question: How reliable is the N62B40 compared to the M62?
items.answer: The N62B40 is generally less reliable than the M62 in terms of valve stem seals and gasket durability, but more refined, lighter, and more fuel-efficient. The valve stem seal issue is the primary concern; if addressed proactively, the N62 can be relatively robust. However, cooling system issues are common across both families. Regular servicing (every 8,000 miles or annually) and cooling system inspection are critical. Many specialists recommend proactively replacing the valve stem seals and water pump on higher‑mileage N62s.
